newsitem.title: ITALY: Armani pares down male silhouette for leaner look.
newsitem.headline: Armani pares down male silhouette for leaner look.

text.p: Giorgio Armani, the Italian designer famous for suits which accentuated the dimensions of the male body, pared down his tailoring for a leaner look in his 1997/98 autumn/winter collection on Thursday.
The silver-haired stylist, closing the Milan ready-to-wear shows, unveiled the slimfit Emporio Armani and Giorgio Armani designs saying his man for the season was in search of subtlety.
"The man is a modern man, subtle not so much in physical form but in the mind. He's looking for much more sophisticated detail," he said backstage after the show at his palazzo in central Milan.
Trousers were narrow, keeping close to the curve of the leg, with no belt or pleats but with pressed creases and turn-ups.
Jackets had lightly padded shoulders, narrower lapels and often no vents at the back, fitting snugly over the body with front fastenings concealed or reduced to one or two buttons.
Navy, charcoal grey and black dominated, with shirts often the same hue and ties made from the same wool as the jacket, while suits came in chalk stripes and subtler patterns.
Less formal attire included short cropped jackets, longer belted ones, pea coats and trench coats in leather and suede, and leafy gold prints on green and blue shirts.

Armani also showed a line of baggy-waisted golf slacks with a leather strap at the ankle and braces, tapered ski pant-style slacks tucked into boots and his Neve (Snow) line of ski gear in matt and glossy green or ice white and black.
Velvet featured in dark tones for suits, blazers and trousers as well as in printed scarves tied snugly at the neck.
Earlier, Briton Katherine Hamnett had a distinctly early 1970s London feel to her collection backed up by a medley of hits by The Rolling Stones.

Suits had moderately broad shoulders with lightly tailored waists and came in broad chalk and pinstripes matched with red, blue and white striped shirts and hats similar to the now-extinct bowler once worn by City bankers and stockbrokers.

Accessories were cravats, thick black-rimmed spectacles, long woollen scarfs wound once round the neck and a variety of caps, including an eccentric English tweed deerstalker with front and back peaks and side flaps tied at the crown.
Velvet was also the look here, with a green double-breasted suit and silk handkerchief protruding from a breast pocket as well as velvet pants.
Armani marked the end of five days of shows which saw few celebrities except for U.S. actor Larry Hagman, noted for his role as dastardly oil baron "Jr" in television series Dallas.
Actor Christopher Lambert was due to attend a later Armani viewing shortly before the world premier in Milan of his latest film "Nirvana".
